text: Erasure, from last lesson, is one of several rights an individual — a data subject — can invoke over their own personal data. This lesson covers the full set, and how an organization actually fulfills one of these requests.

The common set includes access — a copy of the data held about them — rectification, correcting inaccurate data, erasure, portability — receiving their data to move elsewhere — restriction, and objection. Treating every one of these as the same generic bucket is a mistake; an access request and a portability request expect different outputs.

Regardless of which right is invoked, the process is the same four steps. Verify identity first — skipping this turns a privacy right into an attack vector. Locate the data across every system that holds it. Compile and respond within the applicable window. And log the request, independent of the data itself, as proof it was honored.

Locating the data is usually where this breaks down. Personal data is rarely in one table — it's in the application database, a warehouse copy, a CRM, support tools, log files, and sometimes spreadsheets nobody officially sanctioned. A credible process depends on already knowing where personal data lives, which is exactly what classification and a data inventory exist to make possible.
Next lesson: auditing and logging — the record that proves any of this, from access control to DSR fulfillment, actually happened the way you say it did.
